etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From English career. The use of キャ for transcription here is rather peculiar given that it is typically used for the English sequence /kæ/ which is absent in the original English pronunciation. The pitch accent also somewhat indicates that this transcription is more suitable for English carrier, though Japanese pitch accent isn't known for consistently corresponding to English stress.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Appears from the Taishō period in the early 1900s.
Compound of ぱちん (pachin, onomatopoeia for a small hard thing striking something else; compare English kaching) + 子 (-ko, suffix used to form nouns, often diminutive).
A pinball-like children's game was first called ガチャンコ (gachanko) of similar derivation, with this more gambling-oriented machine becoming popular from around 1947.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese verb 捧ぐ (sasagu), a contraction of 差し上ぐ (sasiagu), whence also modern Japanese 差し上げる (sashiageru).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From classical shimo nidan katsuyō verb 据う (suu), possibly parsed as *suwu. In the Muromachi period, there also exists a classical verb 据ゆ (suyu).
Compare 座る (suwaru, “sit”, intransitive).

▲
Sanskrit दान (dāna)bor.

Japanese 旦那
From Middle Chinese 旦那 (MC tanH na), 檀那 (MC dan na), both used as transliterations of Sanskrit दान (dā́na, “generosity, giving, donating”). Ultimately cognate with English donate and donor, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₃nom.
Attested in Japanese sinophone sources since at least the 1000s and in vernacular Japanese sources since at least 1287.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨naɡi₁sa⟩ → */naɡʲisa/ → /naɡisa/
From Old Japanese.
Possibly a compound of 凪(な)ぎ (nagi, “calming, dying down”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 凪(な)ぐ (nagu, “to calm down, to die down”, as of waves or wind), cognate with 和(なご)やか (nagoyaka, “calm, quiet”)) + 磯(さ) (sa, “rocky shore, pebble beach”), where sa is an ancient alternative for so, the abbreviated combining reading of modern 磯(いそ) (iso), cognate with 石(いし) (ishi, “rock, stone”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨mi₁ ki₁pa⟩ → */mʲiɡʲipa/ → /miɡifa/ → /miɡiwa/
Compound of 水(み) (mi, “water”, combining form of 水(みず) (mizu)) + 際(きわ) (kiwa, “edge, boundary”). The kiwa changes to giwa as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/kuroputo/ → */kurofuto/ → /kurouto/
Compound of 玄(くろ) (kuro, “deep, profound”) + 人(うと) (-uto, “person”).
The term 人 (hito, “person”) appears in various older compounds with a root form of 人 (*puto → *buto → *udo, *puto → *futo → *uto). This form is never seen in isolation, and it often undergoes further phonetic changes to combine with preceding vowels. Compare the formation of 仲人 (nakōdo), from naka + udo; 旅人 (tabiudo), from tabi + udo; 素人 (shirōto), from shiro + uto.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 美 (MC mijX).
The use of this character as a suffix in given names is an ateji (当て字) for the native Japanese syllable み (mi), capitalizing on the character’s meaning of “beauty”. Morphologically, this み (mi) typically stems from one of three sources:
* The Old Japanese feminine suffix み (‐mi).
* The nominalizing suffix み (‐mi) attached to adjective stems (such as 宏 (hiro‐, “broad”) in 宏美 (Hiromi)).
* The continuative form (連用形 (ren’yōkei)) of verbs ending in む (‐mu) (such as 恵む (megumu, “to bless”) becoming the noun 恵み (megumi, “blessing”) in 恵美 (Megumi)).
